title: How Things Fail
description: Metal parts fail in recognisable ways, and each leaves clues on the broken face. Use real failure photos to identify fatigue, brittle cleavage, ductile overload, corrosion, and creep.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: A part has broken in service. Before anyone replaces it, why is the fracture surface photographed?

options.text: Because it records where the crack started, which way it ran, and by what mechanism
Because it is the only way to check the alloy against its chemical specification
Because the surface texture reveals the part's manufacturing date
Because hardness can only be measured on a freshly broken face

questions.explanation:
Fractography treats the broken face as evidence. It can reveal where a crack began, how it grew, whether it spread at once or over many cycles, and sometimes the environment around it. Handling, rubbing the halves together, or wire-brushing the surface can destroy that record, so photograph it first.

The useful questions are what happened and whether it will happen again. Replacing the part without reading the fracture surface answers neither.

questions.title: This aluminium specimen was pulled until it came apart. What does the waisted, thinned shape just below each broken end tell you?

images.alt: Two halves of a fractured aluminium tensile specimen held between finger and thumb, each end narrowing to a thinned waist below the break.
images.caption: Tensile test of an AlMgSi aluminium alloy. Photo by Sigmund, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Al_tensile_test.jpg).

images.alt: Two panels. The ductile bar has a thinned waist at the break and interlocking cup-and-cone faces; the brittle bar breaks flat at full width with faces that fit back together.
images.caption: Necking or no necking is the first thing to look for, and you can see it without any instrument.

options.text: The metal stretched and thinned a long way before anything separated
The specimen was machined with a taper before the test began
The break happened instantly, with no plastic flow at all
The alloy was too hard to deform, so it sheared off

questions.explanation:
The narrow waist is necking. After a tensile specimen reaches its ultimate strength, deformation concentrates in one band. That band thins until it tears. Visible necking is the clearest sign of a ductile failure.

A ductile part may sag, bulge, or narrow before it breaks, absorbing substantial energy. Designers value that visible warning because it gives people time to react.

questions.title: These two halves of a cast-iron specimen have flat, granular faces and still measure the full original diameter. What kind of failure is that?

images.alt: Two upright halves of a broken cast-iron tensile specimen photographed side by side, each with a flat, sparkling, granular fracture face at full bar diameter.
images.caption: A cast-iron tensile specimen: flat faces, full section, no waist. Photo by Sigmund, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cast_iron_tensile_test.JPG).

options.text: Brittle fracture. It separated with almost no plastic deformation
Ductile overload, with the necking hidden inside the specimen
Fatigue, after millions of small load cycles
Creep rupture after a long time at high temperature

questions.explanation:
A brittle fracture crosses the full section with no necking. The halves fit together because little material moved, and the break absorbs far less energy than a ductile one.

Brittleness depends on conditions. Steel can behave ductilely when warm, loaded slowly, and smoothly shaped, yet turn brittle when cold, loaded quickly, or notched. Low temperatures and sharp corners caused failures in several early all-welded ships despite ordinary structural steel and loads.

questions.title: Why does the outer rim of a ductile tensile fracture slope at roughly 45° to the pulling direction?

images.alt: A necked bar broken into two interlocking halves beside a circular fracture face showing a stippled fibrous centre ringed by a sloping shear lip.
images.caption: The centre tears open by microvoids joining; the rim runs out along the plane of maximum shear.

options.text: Because that is the plane on which shear stress is highest
Because that is the angle at which the test machine grips the specimen
Because it is a machining artefact left over from turning the bar
Because the rim cools faster than the centre and contracts at an angle

questions.explanation:
When a bar is pulled along its axis, shear stress peaks on planes tilted 45° to it. In a ductile fracture, voids join through the centre first. The crack then reaches the surface along those maximum-shear planes, leaving an angled rim.

This creates the classic *cup and cone*: one half has a shallow cup and the other a matching cone. A fibrous centre and sloping shear lip on a round bar strongly indicate ductile overload.

questions.title: This fracture surface is covered in shallow cavities a few micrometres across. What formed them?

images.alt: Electron micrograph of a steel fracture surface covered in overlapping cup-shaped cavities a few micrometres wide, with a fifteen micrometre scale bar.
images.caption: Ductile dimpled fracture in steel. Photo by Hausild, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tv%C3%A1rn%C3%BD_lom.jpg).

options.text: Voids opened at particles inside the metal, grew under load, and merged
Gas bubbles that were trapped when the metal was cast
Corrosion pits etched into the surface after the part broke
Whole grains that were pulled apart along their boundaries

questions.explanation:
This is *microvoid coalescence*. Plastic strain opens voids at inclusions and second-phase particles. The voids grow until the walls between them join into a crack. Each dimple is half of a void, so the two fracture faces do not fit together.

Round dimples indicate tension. Elongated dimples that point in opposite directions on the two halves indicate shear. Cleaner metal has fewer inclusions where voids can begin, so controlling inclusions can improve toughness.

questions.title: This surface is a mosaic of flat, shiny facets, each carrying a fan of fine lines. Which mechanism does that indicate?

images.alt: Micrograph of a low-carbon steel fracture surface made of flat angular facets at many orientations, each crossed by fine branching river lines.
images.caption: Brittle cleavage in low-carbon steel, imaged with a confocal laser scanning microscope. Photo by DanilovVA, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_brittle_fracture_surface_of_low-carbon_steel.jpg).

options.text: Cleavage. The crack split crystal planes through the grains
Microvoid coalescence, seen at low magnification
Fatigue striations from repeated loading
Cavities forming on grain boundaries during creep

questions.explanation:
Cleavage separates specific crystal planes instead of tearing the metal plastically. Each grain forms a flat facet. Because neighbouring grains have different orientations, the facets catch light at different angles and look crystalline.

The fine lines are *river patterns*. They form where the crack steps between planes at different levels, then merge in the direction of growth. Body-centred cubic metals such as ferritic steel cleave readily when cold, notched, or loaded quickly. Face-centred cubic metals such as austenitic stainless steel and aluminium generally do not.

questions.title: What distinguishes a transgranular fracture from an intergranular one?

options.text: A transgranular crack cuts through the grains; an intergranular crack follows the boundaries between them
A transgranular crack happens in tension and an intergranular crack happens in compression
A transgranular crack starts at the surface and an intergranular crack starts inside
A transgranular crack is always slow and an intergranular crack is always fast

questions.explanation:
The terms describe the crack path, not its speed or load direction. Cleavage and most fatigue cracks are transgranular: they cut through grains. Intergranular cracks follow grain boundaries, leaving whole grain surfaces that can look like sugar crystals.

Weak grain boundaries point to a cause such as hydrogen, temper embrittlement, sensitisation, creep cavities, liquid-metal attack, or corrosion along the boundaries. That evidence shifts the investigation toward chemistry or heat treatment.

questions.title: What are the fine, parallel ridges covering this fatigue fracture surface called?
questions.description: Answer with the term used in fractography. The scale bar in the image is 15 µm.

images.alt: Electron micrograph of a steel fatigue fracture surface showing dense fields of fine parallel ridges, with a fifteen micrometre scale bar.
images.caption: A field of fatigue striations on steel. Photo by Hausild, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Striace.jpg).

questions.explanation:
These ridges are *striations*. Each forms as the crack front blunts and sharpens during a load cycle. They lie perpendicular to the local growth direction, so they record both direction and rate.

The ridges are micrometres apart and require an electron microscope. Broad bands visible to the naked eye are beach marks, a different feature.

questions.title: In the regime where striations form, how many load cycles does a single striation represent?
questions.explanation:
One striation usually represents one cycle. Its spacing gives the local crack-growth rate in millimetres per cycle, which helps estimate how long the crack grew and the load range behind it.

At very low stress intensity, several cycles may pass before the crack moves far enough to leave a visible ridge. A striation count is therefore a lower bound on cycles. Some alloys, including aluminium alloys and many steels, form clear striations; others do not.

questions.title: Which statements about beach marks and striations are correct?

images.alt: A fracture face with a few broad curved bands beside a magnified panel showing dozens of fine parallel ridges, linked by lines from a small box on the fracture face.
images.caption: Same crack, two scales: what the eye reads as one band is an enormous number of cycles.

options.text: Beach marks are usually visible without a microscope; striations are not
A single beach mark can span thousands or millions of cycles
Beach marks record a change in the loading, such as a shutdown, a rest, or an overload
Beach marks and striations are two names for the same feature at different magnifications
Counting beach marks gives you the number of load cycles the part survived

questions.explanation:
Both features form curved bands around the crack origin, but at very different scales.

Striations are micrometre-scale marks, usually one per cycle. Beach marks, also called arrest or clamshell marks, are millimetre-scale bands caused by a change in loading. A shutdown, new duty cycle, overload, or oxidation during a pause can produce one. Constant-amplitude laboratory loading may leave no beach marks, while hundreds of beach marks can represent hundreds of millions of cycles.

questions.title: This aluminium bicycle crank broke during ordinary riding. Most of the face is bright and rough; a darker region along one edge carries curved lines. What happened?

images.alt: End-on view of a broken aluminium bicycle crank arm. Most of the fracture face is bright and coarsely crystalline; a darker, smoother crescent along the lower edge carries fine curved arrest lines.
images.caption: Fatigue fracture of a bicycle pedal crank: the dark crescent with arrest lines is the fatigue zone, the bright area the final overload. Photo by Lokilech, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pedalarm_Bruch.jpg).

images.alt: A circular fracture face labelled with three numbered zones: an initiation site at the rim, concentric beach marks across most of the section, and a hatched final fast fracture cap.
images.caption: Every fatigue fracture has this three-part structure, whatever the part is.

options.text: A crack grew slowly through the dark region over many pedal strokes, then the rest gave way in one go
The whole section broke at once under a single enormous load
The dark region is where the metal overheated and melted
The crank was bent back and forth by hand until it tore, all in one ride

questions.explanation:
The dark fatigue zone began at the surface and grew over many pedal strokes. Rubbing and oxidation darkened and smoothed it; the curved arrest marks bow away from the origin.

The bright, rough area is the final fast fracture. Once the remaining ligament became too small, an ordinary pedal stroke broke it. The final load was familiar. What changed was how little metal remained to carry it.

questions.title: Two identical shafts both failed by fatigue. One face is nearly all fatigue zone with a sliver of final fast fracture; the other is mostly final fast fracture. What does that difference tell you?

images.alt: Two circular fracture faces side by side. The left has a large shaded fatigue region and a thin final-fracture cap; the right has a small fatigue region and a large final-fracture area.
images.caption: Same part, same failure mode, very different stories about the load it was carrying.

options.text: The one with the sliver was running at a lower stress
The one with the sliver was made from a weaker alloy
The one with the sliver was running at a higher temperature
Nothing useful; the ratio is random

questions.explanation:
A fatigue crack grows until the remaining metal cannot carry the cycle's peak load. Under low stress, the crack must consume most of the section first, leaving a large fatigue zone and a thin final crescent. Under high stress, a smaller crack can trigger failure, so the final overload zone is larger.

Investigators use this ratio as an early clue. A large final zone suggests the intact part was already working near its limit, which points toward the design or duty as well as the crack.

questions.title: A bracket carries a repeated load whose peak is comfortably below the alloy's yield strength. Can it still fail by fatigue?

options.text: Yes. Fatigue cracks grow at nominal stresses far below yield
No, because nothing permanent happens below the yield strength
Only if the bracket is a polymer rather than a metal
Only if it is also above half the melting temperature

questions.explanation:
Nominal stress is an average across the section. At a notch, corner, scratch, or inclusion, local stress can be several times higher. A few grains may yield even when the rest of the part does not. Each cycle leaves some irreversible slip until a crack forms.

A static strength check is therefore not enough for a moving part. Fatigue commonly begins at nominal stresses well below yield and causes most in-service mechanical failures.

questions.title: Where should you look first for the origin of a fatigue crack?

images.alt: Two stepped bars carrying force-flow lines. In the sharp-shouldered bar the lines pile into the square corner, marked with red bursts; in the filleted bar the same lines bend smoothly around a generous radius.
images.caption: Same material, load, and nominal stress. The corner creates a different local stress.

options.text: A sharp internal corner or shoulder with no fillet radius
A keyway, cross-hole, or thread root
A stamped mark, tool witness line, or coarse machined finish
A corrosion pit
The middle of a large, smooth, polished face far from any change of section
A generously radiused transition that was shot peened after machining

questions.explanation:
Fatigue starts where stress concentrates. Section changes, holes, thread roots, keyways, weld toes, stamped marks, and deep machining grooves all raise local stress. A square shoulder can multiply it by three or more; sharper features make it worse.

Most fatigue cracks start at a free surface, so grinding marks, corrosion, and handling damage also matter. Generous radii and polished transitions reduce the peak stress. Shot peening adds residual compression at the surface, making it harder for each cycle to open a crack.

questions.title: A steel bracket and an aluminium bracket both survive ten million cycles on the test rig. Why is that result worth less for the aluminium one?

images.alt: An S-N plot with cycles to failure on a logarithmic axis. The steel curve reaches a horizontal fatigue limit; the aluminium curve keeps falling.
images.caption: The flat shelf is the whole difference: one material has a stress you can live under indefinitely, the other does not.

options.text: Aluminium alloys have no fatigue limit, so the S-N curve keeps falling and longer tests still find failures
Aluminium is not affected by cyclic loading in the first place
Fatigue data for aluminium is only meaningful below ten thousand cycles
Aluminium gets stronger the longer it is cycled

questions.explanation:
Plain carbon and low-alloy steels usually develop a knee in the S-N curve around one to ten million cycles. Below this *fatigue limit*, life is effectively unlimited.

Aluminium alloys, copper alloys, and austenitic stainless steels have no such knee. Their curves keep falling, so every stress amplitude has a finite life. Engineers must state fatigue strength at a specific cycle count. Aluminium airframes therefore use finite design lives, retirement times, and inspection intervals instead of relying on an endurance limit.

questions.title: The left half of this image shows a coated buried gas pipeline; the right half is the same area after the corrosion product was blasted away. Why do engineers worry more about pitting than about uniform rusting?

images.alt: Two-panel photograph of a buried steel gas pipeline: on the left a dark patch of corrosion product on green coating beside a ruler, on the right the same area after abrasive blasting, showing shallow pits in bare steel.
images.caption: Before and after blasting: the pits were invisible until the corrosion product came off. Photo by Derek Mawhinney, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Corrosion.Pit.jpg).

options.text: A pit removes very little metal overall, yet it can perforate the wall at a single point
Pits spread across the surface faster than uniform corrosion does
Pits change the chemical composition of the alloy around them
Uniform corrosion cannot be measured, whereas pits can

questions.explanation:
Uniform corrosion thins a surface at a fairly predictable rate. Engineers can measure it by weight loss or wall thickness and allow for it in the design. Pitting concentrates similar metal loss in a few spots, so a pipe can lose little total mass yet develop a leak.

Pits can hide under coatings, scale, or corrosion products until cleaning exposes them. Each pit is also a sharp notch where fatigue or stress corrosion cracking can begin.

questions.title: Galvanised steel pipework is joined straight onto brass and copper fittings, with water inside. Which metal corrodes?

images.alt: A wall-mounted water meter manifold in galvanised steel pipe joined to brass valves and copper pipework, with rust staining concentrated at the joints between the two metals.
images.caption: Galvanised steel joined directly to copper and brass, with the attack showing at the joints. Photo by Manuel Capdevila, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Steel-copper_galvanic_corrosion.jpg).

options.text: The zinc and steel. The less noble metal becomes the anode and dissolves
The copper and brass, because they are the softer metals
Both, at the same rate, since they sit in the same water
Neither, as long as the water is clean and fresh

questions.explanation:
Two metals in electrical contact with the same electrolyte form a battery. The less noble metal becomes the anode, gives up electrons, and dissolves. The nobler cathode is protected.

Galvanising uses this effect deliberately. Zinc corrodes before steel and protects it even through scratches. Sacrificial anodes on hulls and water heaters work the same way. At an unwanted dissimilar-metal joint, a dielectric union breaks the electrical path.

questions.title: Two joints sit in seawater: steel bolts holding a large copper plate, and copper bolts holding a large steel plate. Which one is the dangerous design?

images.alt: Two panels comparing a large anodic plate with three small cathodic fasteners against a large cathodic plate with three small anodic fasteners marked with red crosses.
images.caption: The metals are identical in both panels. Only the area ratio is reversed, and that is what decides the outcome.

options.text: The steel bolts in the copper plate
The copper bolts in the steel plate
Both equally, because the metals are the same in each case
Neither, because a bolt is always the cathode

questions.explanation:
Area controls the corrosion rate. A large cathode can drive substantial current, while a small anode concentrates that current into little metal.

Steel bolts in a copper plate form a small anode beside a large cathode, so the bolts corrode quickly. With copper bolts in a steel plate, corrosion spreads across the large steel plate. Avoid pairing a small piece of the less noble metal with a large piece of the nobler one. Steel fasteners in copper roofing or graphite composites are common examples of this trap.

questions.title: Fine branching cracks run out from a welded collar in this vessel wall. What has to be present at the same time for stress corrosion cracking?

images.alt: A cut section of vessel wall beside a welded collar, its surface covered by a dense network of fine branching cracks spreading out from the weld.
images.caption: Stress corrosion cracking driven by residual stress from an unsuitable welded reinforcement collar. Photo by CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Stress-Corrosion-Cracking-caused-by-weld-stress-01.jpg).

images.alt: Three overlapping circles labelled sustained tensile stress, susceptible alloy, and specific chemical environment, with stress corrosion cracking sitting only in the central overlap.
images.caption: The failure lives only in the middle. Removing any one circle is a valid fix.

options.text: A sustained tensile stress, which can come entirely from residual welding stress
An alloy that is susceptible to the particular environment involved
A specific chemical environment, such as chlorides for austenitic stainless steel
A load that cycles rapidly back and forth
A temperature above the alloy's melting point

questions.explanation:
Stress corrosion cracking needs sustained tensile stress, a susceptible alloy, and a specific chemical environment. Remove any one and the cracking stops.

Residual stress from welding or cold forming can supply enough tension without an applied load, so SCC often appears near welds. The alloy and environment must match: austenitic stainless steel cracks in hot chlorides but resists ammonia, while brass does the opposite. Fine, branching cracks with little surrounding deformation are a common visual clue.

questions.title: A steel component with a long, clean service record starts failing early after the equipment is moved to a damp, salty site. The duty cycle has not changed. What is the likeliest explanation?

images.alt: Three panels: a sound surface under cyclic load, the same surface with a corrosion pit forming a notch, and a fatigue crack growing down from the root of that pit.
images.caption: Corrosion supplies the notch; the ordinary cyclic load does the rest.

options.text: Corrosion pits are forming and acting as ready-made crack starters
Salt water lowers the alloy's melting point
The humidity has increased the load the component carries
Steel loses its yield strength when it gets wet

questions.explanation:
A corrosion pit is a sharp notch where a fatigue crack can start. In a corrosive environment, pits shorten or remove the long crack-initiation stage.

Corrosion fatigue can also remove steel's fatigue limit. The S-N curve keeps falling instead of flattening, so a stress that was safe in dry air now has a finite life. The design may need a specified service life, protective coating, or cathodic protection.

questions.title: A turbine blade under a constant load well below its yield strength slowly stretches over thousands of hours in service. What is that called?

images.alt: A strain-versus-time curve in three shaded bands: a decelerating primary stage, a long straight secondary stage, and an accelerating tertiary stage ending at a rupture cross.
images.caption: Most of the life is spent in the straight middle section. Once the curve turns upward there is very little left.

options.text: Creep
Fatigue
Cleavage
Work hardening

questions.explanation:
Creep is plastic deformation that develops over time under a steady load. It has three stages. The primary rate slows as the metal hardens. The secondary stage runs at a steady minimum rate and occupies most of the life. In the tertiary stage, damage accelerates toward rupture.

The design limit may be strain rather than fracture. A turbine blade can touch its casing after creeping a fraction of a millimetre. A crept bolted flange can lose clamping force and leak before anything breaks.

questions.title: Creep becomes a design concern above roughly what fraction of a metal's absolute melting temperature?
questions.description: Answer as a decimal fraction, for example `0.25`. Both temperatures are measured in kelvin.
questions.explanation:
*Homologous temperature* is service temperature divided by melting temperature, both in kelvin. Above roughly 0.4, atomic diffusion becomes fast enough for creep to matter.

Steel melts near 1700 K, so this threshold is around 400 °C. Boiler tubes, steam pipes, and turbine blades can therefore be limited by creep, while a room-temperature steel bracket is not. Lead melts near 600 K, putting a lead roof near 0.5 at ordinary temperatures, so it can creep over decades. Solder joints and polymers face the same issue.

questions.title: In the tertiary stage of creep the strain rate accelerates. Why?

options.text: Grain-boundary cavities and local thinning reduce the section carrying the load
The applied load is deliberately increased at that point in the test
The metal has begun to melt
The temperature is raised at the end to finish the test sooner

questions.explanation:
The load stays constant, but the material changes. Cavities form and join along grain boundaries while the section thins. Less metal carries the same force, raising the true stress and speeding further damage until rupture.

High-temperature equipment must be inspected for cavities and swelling during the secondary stage. Once tertiary creep begins, little service life remains.

questions.title: Which of these failure modes typically give little or no outward warning before the part separates?

options.text: Brittle cleavage fracture
Fatigue, right up until the final fast fracture
Stress corrosion cracking
Ductile overload

questions.explanation:
Ductile overload usually gives warning. The part bends, sags, bulges, or necks while absorbing substantial energy. Designers may prefer this behaviour even if it costs some strength.

Brittle fracture can cross a sound-looking part near the speed of sound. Fatigue cracks remain hidden for most of their growth. Stress corrosion cracks are fine, branching, and often concealed by scale or coating. These modes require damage-tolerant design and scheduled crack detection with methods such as dye penetrant, magnetic particle inspection, or ultrasonics.

questions.title: A shaft that ran for three years snaps. Two thirds of the face is smooth with fine curved lines; the rest is rough. There is no necking anywhere. What is the diagnosis, and where should the fix go?

options.text: Fatigue under an ordinary repeated load. Remove the stress raiser at the crack origin
Ductile overload. Specify a stronger alloy
Brittle fracture from a single impact. Fit a guard
Creep. Reduce the operating temperature

questions.explanation:
Three years of service makes a one-off overload unlikely. The smooth zone and curved arrest lines indicate fatigue, while the rough zone is the final fast fracture. No necking means it was not a slow ductile tear. The large fatigue zone also suggests fairly low nominal stress.

The fix belongs at the crack origin. With a notch present, steel's fatigue strength stops tracking its tensile strength, and stronger steels may be more notch-sensitive. Better fixes include a larger fillet, smoother finish, shot peening, a redesigned keyway, or a lower stress range.
